newsitem.title: USA: Kansas wheat crop slowly recovering from freeze.
newsitem.headline: Kansas wheat crop slowly recovering from freeze.

text.p: The Kansas wheat crop is slowly recovering from the hard freeze of April 12-13 and secondary tillers have begun showing up in the areas affected by the cold snap, crop scouts said.
The scouts are touring U.S. hard red winter wheat growing areas this week in the annual Wheat Quality Council tour.

T.J. Byrum, chief statistician for the Kansas Agricultural Statistics Service, said there was no doubt the Kansas wheat crop was hurt by the cold weather but there was reason to be optimistic. "There are secondary tillers forming," he said.
Each tiller of a wheat plant is a potential head of wheat which eventually will fill with wheat berries or grain.
The mid-April cold spell damaged or killed a significant number of plants and primary tillers in fields of southwest Kansas and in the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles.

But Byrum and others declined to offer a preliminary estimate of the amount of wheat harmed by the cold snap, which left the industry reeling and wheat futures soaring. Early loss estimates ranged from roughly 50 million bushels to as much as 300 million.
The U.S. Agriculture Department weekly crop report for Kansas issued on Monday rated the crop in the top wheat growing state with minor changes from last week.

Eleven percent of the crop was in the poor to very poor category, up from 14 percent a week earlier. But the amount of wheat rated in fair condition rose 3 points to 34 percent and the amount rated excellent also rose 5 points to 8 percent. That was shifted from the "good" category, where the rating fell 5 points to 47 percent from 52 percent.
But there were some crop observers who expressed concern about dwindling soil moisture levels in portions of Kansas.
"The concern is going to be how dry it is out west," Mark Nelson, Agricultural Economist for the Kansas Farm Bureau, told the tour's preparatory meeting here on Monday night.
"I came back from Colby yesterday and the western one-third is struggling on a moisture basis, not terribly, but the topsoil is getting pretty short," Nelson said.
Monday's weekly crop report for Kansas rated the topsoil moisture level in the state as of Sunday at 11 percent short, above the eight percent in that category the previous week.
In the Northwest District, 44 percent of the topsoil moisture was rated short along with 33 percent of subsoils.
Nelson said that current Kansas weather was conducive for a partial recovery of the crop but the jury was still out.
"You're going to have to wait. The crop was in varying stages of development when it froze," Nelson said.
"The weather has been very good and it's going to be a waiting game. If we get a hot and dry last half of May, it could hurt the secondary tillers," he added.
The tour on Tuesday will travel from Manhattan to Colby and on Wednesday the group will be in southwest and south-central Kansas, where the freeze hit hardest.
On Thursday the tour moves from Wichita to Kansas City where an overall crop assessment will be announced on Thursday afternoon at the Kansas City Board of Trade.
